Also, differently from Study 2, stereotypes were widely shared
in our sample, with the large majority of participants endorsing
traditional gender and age stereotypes. In fact 83% of the Italian-
speakers and 84% of the Arabic-speakers considered males/young
people as more agentic than females/old people.
Spatial positioning
We ﬁrst ran a preliminary 2 (native language: Italian vs. Ara-
bic) = 2 (category: male/female vs. young/old) = 2 (order of men-
tioning: agentic group ﬁrst vs. second) ANOVA in which the last
two factors were repeated measures, using the spatial positioning
score as the dependent variable. This analysis showed that cate-
gory had no effect either in itself or in interaction with the remain-
ing variables (all F’s < 1), suggesting that ﬁndings for males vs.
females did not differ from those for young vs. old people. We
therefore collapsed the two target categories.

Importantly, as with attention residue in Study 1a, the analyses
for performance in Study 1b revealed a signiﬁcant Task A fram-
ing  Task B framing interaction on both recall (F(1,73) = 4.00,
p < 0.05, g2 = 0.05) and editorial mistakes (F(1,73) = 5.82, p < 0.05,
g2 = 0.07). As illustrated in Table 5 and Fig. 2, the nature of this
interaction supports Hypothesis 4: the effects of Task A framing
were dependent upon the framing of Task B. When Task B was pro-
motion framed, performance on that task was signiﬁcantly lower
when Task A was prevention- rather than promotion-framed (t
(36) = 3.22, p < 0.01, Cohen d’s = 1.05 for recall and t(36) = 3.53,
p 6 0.001, Cohen d’s = 1.14 for editorial mistakes). However, when
Task B was prevention framed, the effects of Task A framing were
reduced and non-signiﬁcant, such that performance on Task B
was improved and at comparable levels independently from Task
A framing (see Table 5).

Participants were randomly assigned to one of the six scenarios, and
as in previous studies they were asked to imagine that the actor “willful-
ly and intentionally” engaged in the act. As in Study 1, the likelihood in-
dices were reliable: harmful (α = 0.94), impure-sexual (α = 0.94). In
the appraisal block, three items assessed wrongness using the same
items as Study 1 (α = 0.87). The order of the likelihood and appraisal
blocks was randomized.

on their industry-speciﬁc knowledge (Kor & Sundaramurthy, 2009;
Pennings, Lee, & Wattleoostuijn, 1998) as it provides links with industry
players and can help recruit candidates for top positions (Hillman &
Dalziel, 2003). Industry knowledge equips directors to reduce the risk
of adverse selection (Shen & Cannella, 2002) and develop TMT human
capital. They are familiar with needed top management skills and the
information required (Filatotchev, 2006; Hillman & Dalziel, 2003), un-
derstand ﬁrm operations, and are more effective in assisting TMTs
with strategic decisions (Mooney, Dalton, Dalton, & Certo, 2007).
Thus, rent generation capabilities are likely greater when the board
includes outsiders with industry experience to facilitate understanding
of ﬁrm operations and lower information and knowledge asymmetries.
This arrangement may improve the evaluation of decisions and perfor-
mance and mitigate TMTs’ rent appropriation (Anderson & Reeb, 2004;
Kor & Sundaramurthy, 2009), yet motivate development and deploy-
ment of human capital.
